title: Sumedha in the mud
hook: a hermit lies down in the mud so the past Buddha Dipankara can walk over him, and vows to awaken (Jataka, the introduction)

segments.voice: Yesterday, how a Jataka works: a story now, a story long ago, and a last line, the samodhana, naming who each character was. Your line was who was who. Did you notice an old pattern showing up again? Today, the story the tales grow out of. Day eight hundred seventeen.

Mud. A stretch of road still soft and wet, and a Buddha walking toward it. The introduction to the Jataka opens long before Siddhartha, with a hermit named Sumedha. A city is preparing its road for the Buddha Dipankara, and Sumedha has asked for a piece of it to make smooth himself. He hasn't finished. The mud is still there when Dipankara and his monks arrive. So Sumedha does something nobody asked of him. That moment is today.
screen: `A ROAD NOT FINISHED.` → `A HERMIT NAMED SUMEDHA.` → `THE BUDDHA ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First, who Sumedha was. In the story he's born rich, and one day he looks at the treasure his family left him and thinks: they gathered all this, and not one of them took a coin along when they died. So he gives it away and goes to the mountains to live as a hermit. The mud scene starts with empty hands. Second, the mud. As Dipankara comes near, Sumedha loosens his hair, spreads his rough hermit's garment over the wet ground, and lies down in it, face down, so the Buddha and the monks can walk across him and keep their feet clean. It's a strange, physical act. Not a speech. A body on a road. Third, the choice. Lying there, the text says, Sumedha knows he could end his own suffering in this very life if he wished. And he turns it down. What use is crossing over alone, he thinks. He'd rather become a Buddha himself, and carry others across with him. That's the vow: a longer road, chosen on purpose, for other people. Fourth, the answer. Dipankara stops beside him, looks far ahead, and declares that this hermit will one day be a Buddha named Gotama. The crowd hears it. Sumedha stands up. The Jataka's introduction sets the tales that follow on the long road from this vow. Mahayana traditions teach a bodhisattva vow too, in their own words and forms. In this story, the road begins with a man in the dirt, and a promise said silently.
screen: `FIRST HE GAVE IT ALL AWAY.` · `HE LAY DOWN IN THE MUD.` · `HE CHOSE THE LONGER ROAD.` · `DIPANKARA SAW AND SPOKE.` · then, large: `THE VOW IN THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one quiet vow. Not a grand one. Something small you could actually keep, aimed at someone besides yourself. Making a little more room for one person this week. Answering one message with patience. Choose it now, and say it once, silently, the way Sumedha did in the mud, with nobody watching. Then let it go and just breathe. You don't have to feel anything special. A vow can be quiet and still be real. The bell holds the time.
Bodhisatta. The being on the way to awakening: what Sumedha vowed to become when he lay down in the mud before the Buddha Dipankara, awakening not alone, but for others. Today's word.
Your line: the vow in the mud. Once today, when there's a quick way for you and a slower way that helps someone else, notice the choice. Then pick on purpose. Day eight hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities the story of Sumedha and Dipankara is told as the start of the Buddha's long path, and in Mahayana communities bodhisattva vows are taken in ceremonies and recited in practice.

fork.setup: you're Sumedha, face down in the mud. you know you could end your own suffering in this life. what do you choose?
options: end it now. it's what you came for.
vow to become a Buddha and carry others across.
get up and finish smoothing the road.
fork.reveal: he turns down his own crossing and vows the longer road, and Dipankara declares he will one day be the Buddha Gotama.

original.note: Pali bodhisatta: the being on the way to awakening. the tales use it for the future Buddha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a humble hermit lets someone walk on him.
what it means: Sumedha turns down an awakening he could have had then, and vows to become a Buddha for others.
what a scholar hears: the Jataka's introduction sets the start of the bodhisatta's long path at this vow before Dipankara, and the numbered tales that follow are read as steps along it.

sources.ref: Jataka, introduction (Nidanakatha, the distant epoch: Sumedha and Dipankara)

notes: Confirm the Nidanakatha details: Sumedha reflects that his ancestors took none of their treasure with them, gives it away, becomes a hermit; asks for a stretch of road for Dipankara, it is unfinished; loosens his hair, spreads his garment (bark/antelope skin) over the mud and lies face down; reflects he could attain arahantship that day but chooses Buddhahood to carry others across; Dipankara declares he will become the Buddha Gotama.
Deliberately no time spans (asankheyyas/kalpas) and no counts stated.
The Mahayana bodhisattva-vow sentence and howItsDone are general descriptions; confirm the wording is fair to both traditions.
